title: Episode 12: When Playing Board Games is my Least Favorite Part of the Hobby
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DDiDtP-uOqU

An unusually blunt confession, and the argument underneath it is the sharpest thing in the early Hobbycast. Daniel (@dungeondive) likes buying, collecting, reading about and talking about board games — and sometimes the actual playing is the least enjoyable part. He is careful about why. It is not laziness; it is a ratio. Board games demand a great deal of effort before they return any pleasure.

Every other medium he loves has standards. A new book needs no instruction. A DVD player works the way the last one did. A third-person video game puts movement on the left stick and the camera on the right, because *Doom*, *Half-Life* and *Halo* settled those conventions decades ago. Board games settled nothing. Ninety per cent of his shelf is the same genre and almost every box plays by different rules — three games with square grids disagree about whether diagonals are adjacent.

His proposal: license engines. Let a well-documented system be reused so designers spend their effort on art, world, story and character — the things players actually remember — instead of redesigning movement. He notes Games Workshop did the opposite with four incompatible modern *Warhammer Quest* titles, and credits the OSR's shared foundations for why he's drifting toward small RPGs.

----

Would shared engines make dungeon crawls better, or just make them all feel the same?
